title: What the Machine Invented: Mining New Mathematical Instruments from OpenAI's October 2026 Release of AI-Generated Mathematics
authors: Ying Xie
abstract: On 6 October 2026 OpenAI published an initial 722 AI-written mathematical manuscripts, organized into 372 problem families, in the public repository github.com/openai/math. The release includes claimed solutions to many prominent open problems. We approach this collection as a treasure mine of mathematical ideas. Our aim is to extract new lemmas, constructions, inequalities and proof mechanisms introduced in the source arguments, and to distinguish them from established tools and new combinations of those tools. We call these mathematical instruments. Extraction comes first; their validity, novelty and possible reuse then become subjects for further study. The resulting descriptions also help readers understand the selected papers without having to reconstruct every argument at the outset. We examine 38 families in two groups of 17 and 21, spanning number theory, geometry, analysis, combinatorics, complexity, algebra, operator algebras, topology and mathematical physics. Each entry records the claim, extracted instruments, antecedents and caveats. Eleven cross-cutting patterns connect the entries, and a scoreboard records formalization status and dependencies. Novelty assessments are provisional and sometimes mixed. Selected source comparisons correct mathematical statements, hypotheses and counts; they do not independently establish priority or certify the underlying proofs. No Lean development was compiled or kernel-checked for this survey. We also briefly describe a subsequent application of the signed restriction lemma from family 112 to circuit lower bounds at every fixed depth.

infographic.key_insight: The paper mines OpenAI’s 2026 AI-generated mathematics release to identify reusable “mathematical instruments” — new lemmas, constructions, inequalities, and proof mechanisms — across 38 problem families.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a structured way to extract, compare, and track candidate proof components that could inform future automated theorem proving and formal verification workflows.
method: Surveyed 38 families from 722 AI-written manuscripts across two groups of 17 and 21
Recorded each family’s claim, extracted instruments, antecedents, and caveats
Added cross-cutting patterns and a scoreboard for formalization status and dependencies
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a corpus-level review spanning 372 problem families, with selected source comparisons and a formalization/dependency scoreboard, but no Lean development was compiled or kernel-checked.
infographic.watch_item: Novelty and correctness assessments are explicitly provisional, and the survey does not independently certify the underlying proofs.
infographic.paper_title: What the Machine Invented: Mining New Mathematical Instruments from OpenAI's October 2026 Release of AI-Generated Mathematics

title: Recursive Gradient Retraction Methods for Stochastic Nonconvex Optimization on Stiefel Manifolds
authors: Zhijie Yuan, Lei Sun, Ganzhao Yuan
abstract: Nonconvex optimization on Stiefel manifolds underlies many problems in machine learning and deep learning. However, existing stochastic Riemannian retraction methods often rely on stepsizes that require prior knowledge of the gradient Lipschitz constant, a prescribed iteration horizon, or restrictive batch-size choices. We develop {\sf RGR}, a recursive gradient retraction method for stochastic nonconvex optimization on Stiefel manifolds. Instead of recursively updating gradient estimators in changing tangent spaces, {\sf RGR} constructs them in the Euclidean space and subsequently maps them to tangent space, thereby avoiding vector transport. The method comprises three variants: {\sf RGR-SPIDER} for finite-sum optimization and {\sf RGR-SRM} and {\sf RGR-EMA} for online stochastic optimization. {\sf RGR-SPIDER} is Lipschitz-free and horizon-free, as its adaptive stepsize requires neither prior knowledge of the gradient Lipschitz constant nor a prescribed iteration horizon. {\sf RGR-SRM} and {\sf RGR-EMA} are mini-batch and horizon-free methods whose convergence guarantees do not rely on prescribed large batch sizes and whose parameters can be chosen without prior knowledge of the total iteration budget. We show that {\sf RGR-SPIDER} reaches an $\varepsilon$-critical point using $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ iterations and $\mathcal{O}(N+\sqrt{N}\varepsilon^{-2})$ component-gradient evaluations, where $N$ denotes the number of component functions. For the online setting, {\sf RGR-SRM} and {\sf RGR-EMA} achieve iteration complexities of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon^{-4})$, respectively. Experiments on principal component analysis, low-rank matrix completion, and orthogonal convolutional neural networks demonstrate faster empirical convergence than methods that construct recursive gradient estimators directly in Riemannian tangent spaces.

infographic.key_insight: RGR builds recursive stochastic gradients in Euclidean space and then retracts them to the Stiefel manifold, removing the need for vector transport while enabling adaptive, horizon-free optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers practical training algorithms for manifold-constrained machine learning models such as PCA, matrix completion, and orthogonal neural networks, with less tuning than prior Riemannian approaches.
method: RGR-SPIDER: finite-sum variant with Lipschitz-free, horizon-free adaptive stepsizes.
RGR-SRM and RGR-EMA: online stochastic variants that are mini-batch free and do not require a preset iteration budget.
Recursive estimator is formed in Euclidean space and mapped to tangent space via retraction, avoiding vector transport.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theory plus experiments on principal component analysis, low-rank matrix completion, and orthogonal convolutional neural networks, showing faster empirical convergence than tangent-space recursive methods.
infographic.watch_item: Performance and stability may still depend on retraction choice and adaptive hyperparameter settings, especially for large-scale manifold-constrained training.
infographic.paper_title: Recursive Gradient Retraction Methods for Stochastic Nonconvex Optimization on Stiefel Manifolds

title: Neural Spline Flow Diffeomorphisms for Pullback Finite Element Methods on Complex Domains
authors: Ioannis Kalogeris, Anaksagoras Spitas, Konstantinos Atzarakis, George Stavroulakis, Vissarion Papadopoulos
abstract: We propose a method for solving partial differential equations on complex domains by learning smooth, invertible mappings from a fixed reference domain using Neural Spline Flows (NSFs). Monotone rational-quadratic spline coupling layers ensure a strictly positive Jacobian determinant by construction, eliminating the need for Jacobian-sign penalties. A diffeomorphic pullback transfers the weak form of the PDE to the reference domain, enabling finite element analysis on reusable structured meshes. To generalize across shapes, a shared NSF is conditioned on low-dimensional latent codes learned through an auto-decoder framework; a subsequent encoder predicts these codes for unseen geometries in a single forward pass. For a given learned map, the pullback preserves the mathematical structure of the PDE and is exactly equivalent to solving on the domain represented by that map. Because the learned domain generally approximates the target geometry, geometric mapping error remains distinct from finite element discretization and quadrature errors. Numerical benchmarks show that sufficiently accurate learned mappings yield reliable finite element solutions. By avoiding repeated generation of unstructured meshes, the method addresses a bottleneck in simulation workflows. The fixed reference mesh also creates opportunities for efficient assembly, memory-aligned data access, and precomputed quadrature. The resulting framework assigns geometric complexity to the neural network while retaining conventional finite element discretization and convergence properties on the learned domain, with overall accuracy also governed by geometric fidelity.

infographic.key_insight: A Neural Spline Flow can learn a smooth, invertible domain map so PDEs on complex geometries can be solved by pulling the problem back to a fixed reference mesh.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This reduces the need for repeated unstructured meshing and enables reusable, structured finite element workflows with potential gains in assembly efficiency, memory access, and quadrature reuse.
method: Use monotone rational-quadratic spline coupling layers to enforce a strictly positive Jacobian determinant.
Transfer the PDE weak form to a reference domain via a diffeomorphic pullback and solve with standard finite elements.
Condition a shared NSF on latent shape codes and predict those codes for new geometries with an encoder.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical benchmarks showing that sufficiently accurate learned mappings produce reliable finite element solutions.
infographic.watch_item: Overall accuracy depends on geometric fidelity, so mapping error must be controlled separately from discretization and quadrature error.
infographic.paper_title: Neural Spline Flow Diffeomorphisms for Pullback Finite Element Methods on Complex Domains

title: Boundary Control of a Modified Timoshenko-Ehrenfest Beam via Reduced-Order Reinforcement Learning
authors: Leonardo R S Rodrigues
abstract: In this paper, we study the active vibration control of an elastic beam using reinforcement learning (RL). The physical system is modeled by a modified Timoshenko-Ehrenfest type linear partial differential equation with simply supported boundary conditions. The dynamics are approximated by a reduced-order model (ROM) obtained through eigenvalue expansion and truncated Galerkin projection. Control is applied through boundary actuation. The resulting finite-dimensional system is formulated as a continuous-time Markov decision process and solved numerically using the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm. All modeling steps, from physical formulation to temporal discretization and control design, are explicitly described. A systematic comparison is performed between the controller learned via PPO and the classical linear quadratic (LQR) regulator. The analysis highlights the strengths and limitations of each approach, both from a theoretical and practical point of view, with particular emphasis on energy dissipation mechanisms and actuator constraints.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that boundary-actuated reinforcement learning can stabilize and damp vibrations in a modified Timoshenko-Ehrenfest beam using a reduced-order PDE model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a data-driven control route for flexible structures where boundary actuation is practical and classical model-based tuning may be difficult.
method: Model the beam with a modified Timoshenko-Ehrenfest linear PDE under simply supported boundary conditions.
Reduce the infinite-dimensional system via eigenvalue expansion and truncated Galerkin projection.
Train a PPO controller on the resulting continuous-time Markov decision process and compare it with LQR.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a systematic numerical comparison between PPO-based control and the classical LQR regulator, with attention to vibration suppression, energy dissipation, and actuator limits.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the reduced-order approximation and discretization, so stability or accuracy may degrade if the truncation misses important beam dynamics.
infographic.paper_title: Boundary Control of a Modified Timoshenko-Ehrenfest Beam via Reduced-Order Reinforcement Learning

title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?
authors: Kaifei Wang, Zikang Shan, Liwei Wang, Yinyu Ye, Han Zhong
abstract: Momentum is a classical tool for accelerating convex optimization and a standard component of modern large language model training. Yet recent empirical work has questioned the usefulness of first-moment momentum in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We study this question through a bandit formulation of RLVR with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum, where the EMA coefficient $β$ controls how quickly the weights on past gradients decay. When policy gradients are evaluated exactly, we prove that increasing $β$ within a range that prevents overshoot strictly accelerates optimization. When gradients are estimated from sampled responses, a positive expected gain can be obscured by sampling fluctuations. We show that as the learning rate $η$ decreases, the expected gain with fixed $β$ vanishes faster than these fluctuations, whereas increasing $β$ to keep $η/(1-β)$ within the safe regime preserves a nonvanishing gain that eventually dominates them. Bandit simulations quantitatively validate these predictions. RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base using SGD with EMA and AdamW support our principle of choosing larger coefficients in practical LLM post-training. On Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, simply increasing $β_1$ improves mean validation accuracy by nearly $2$ percentage points over the conventional choice, demonstrating the principle's effectiveness at a larger model scale.

infographic.key_insight: In RL with verifiable rewards, larger EMA momentum can help—if it is increased enough to stay in a stable, non-overshooting regime.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For LLM post-training and RLVR, tuning momentum upward can yield better sample efficiency and validation accuracy than using conventional small momentum values.
method: Analyze a bandit model of RLVR with bias-corrected EMA momentum.
Prove that, under exact gradients, larger EMA coefficients accelerate optimization before overshoot.
Show that with sampled gradients, keeping η/(1−β) in the safe regime preserves a gain that beats sampling noise as η shrinks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Bandit simulations and RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen2.5-32B (with SGD/EMA and AdamW) validate the theory, including nearly 2 percentage points higher mean validation accuracy from increasing β1.
infographic.watch_item: Momentum must be increased carefully; if the effective step size becomes too large, overshoot can negate the benefit.
infographic.paper_title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?

title: Euler: Towards Human-Centered Multi-Agent Mathematical Discovery
authors: Qiuyu Chen, Qi Wang, Liang Xu, Xin Jin, Baao Xie, Wenjun Zeng
abstract: Mathematical research drives scientific discovery, and recent advances in AI for mathematics have shown that language-model agents can solve challenging problems and develop substantial mathematical proofs. Yet much of today's AI-for-mathematics work centers on obtaining a final answer. This emphasis leaves the exploration behind a result difficult for researchers to understand, while long-running investigations face fragmented context and the risk of unsupported claims propagating across reasoning steps. We present Euler, a human-centered mathematical research system built around a shared, structured representation of the research process. Euler organizes mathematical statements, assumptions, proof dependencies, alternative approaches, failed attempts, and verification evidence into connected research graphs. This representation allows researchers to trace how results are developed and supplies agents with persistent, task-relevant knowledge for planning, collaboration, and verification across sessions. Researchers can also select a graph node linked to a saved team state, revisit the agents' earlier reasoning, and explore alternative directions through continued interaction. We illustrate Euler's capabilities through three mathematical research case studies and describe the implemented system and its software validation.

infographic.key_insight: Euler reframes AI mathematics from single-shot answers to a human-centered, persistent research workflow that records and reuses the full reasoning process.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The system’s research-graph design supports traceability, collaboration, and stateful multi-agent planning, which is useful for long-horizon theorem proving and other complex scientific workflows.
method: Builds a shared research graph of statements, assumptions, proof dependencies, alternatives, failed attempts, and verification evidence.
Lets agents and researchers revisit saved team states and continue exploration from any graph node.
Uses persistent task-relevant context to reduce fragmentation and help prevent unsupported claims from propagating.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports three mathematical research case studies plus implementation and software validation, but does not provide quantitative benchmark results.
infographic.watch_item: The main concern is that the approach appears validated mainly through case studies, so scalability and robustness across larger, harder proof tasks remain to be shown.
infographic.paper_title: Euler: Towards Human-Centered Multi-Agent Mathematical Discovery

title: AI-Assisted Tumor-Growth Law Discovery from Sparse Data: Refitting and LLM-Based Ranking
authors: Yitian Lu, Weinan Wang
abstract: Inferring tumor-growth laws from sparse, noisy observations requires more than accurate curve fitting. We study an AI-assisted workflow involving symbolic regression, mathematical admissibility checks, coefficient refitting, and large language model (LLM) ranking. Synthetic Gompertz data allow trajectory fit, forecasting, and recovery of the governing growth law to be assessed separately. A dense noiseless control recovers the generating family, but sparse noisy sampling frequently leads to alternative forms. Among retained candidates in the tested configurations, physics-informed neural network refitting often increases growth-law error, whereas classical nonlinear least squares usually reduces it. A separate exploratory analysis of archived LLM rankings shows no consistent improvement over selection by training error and identifies errors in mathematical reasoning. Plausible saturation, accurate trajectory fits, and convincing explanations can therefore coexist with incorrect growth laws. Mathematical validity and law recovery require evaluation alongside predictive performance.

infographic.key_insight: Sparse noisy tumor-growth data can produce convincing fits and explanations while still yielding the wrong governing law, so law discovery must be judged beyond prediction accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For scientific modeling workflows, the study shows that coefficient refitting and model ranking should be validated against mathematical correctness, not just curve-fit quality.
method: Symbolic regression generates candidate growth laws from sparse data.
Candidates are filtered by mathematical admissibility and then coefficient-refit using either physics-informed neural networks or nonlinear least squares.
An LLM-based ranking step is compared against selection by training error.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using synthetic Gompertz data, dense noiseless data recover the true family, while sparse noisy sampling often selects alternative forms; nonlinear least squares usually lowers growth-law error, but PINN refitting often increases it.
infographic.watch_item: LLM rankings and high-quality trajectory fits do not guarantee correct law recovery, so downstream selection criteria can be misleading.
infographic.paper_title: AI-Assisted Tumor-Growth Law Discovery from Sparse Data: Refitting and LLM-Based Ranking

title: TPPO: Tracking-Value PPO For Language Model Reasoning
authors: Futing Wang, Chenxi Li, Jianhao Yan, Yun Luo, Zhi Wang, Yizhuo Li
abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is widely used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for language-model reasoning. While \emph{value evolution along trajectory} characterizes relative token-level credit, yet standard critics often fail to track it under sparse terminal rewards. To model this evolution, we analyze the relation between successive prefix values and show that they admit a Bayesian decomposition with additive updates in log-odds space. We use this additive structure to construct Tracking-Value PPO (\method), a cumulative value parameterization that sums position-wise scalar outputs into value logits. These outputs are learned through terminal-outcome supervision on the reconstructed values. \method improves aggregate mathematical reasoning scores over PPO by 7.0 and 8.4 points on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively, while improving out-of-distribution generalization. Gains extend to Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen3.5-9B and to countdown, and scientific coding tasks. Further analysis shows more accurate tracking of value evolution and more reliable advantage estimates. Our code is publicly available in https://github.com/LINs-lab/TPPO.

infographic.key_insight: TPPO replaces a single critic with a cumulative, log-odds-style value decomposition that better tracks how value evolves across a reasoning trajectory under sparse terminal rewards.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives a more faithful reward/advantage signal for training language models on math reasoning, improving PPO stability and generalization without changing the underlying task reward.
method: Decompose successive prefix values with a Bayesian additive update in log-odds space.
Parameterize the value as a sum of position-wise scalar outputs, producing cumulative value logits.
Train these outputs using terminal-outcome supervision on reconstructed values.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports +7.0 and +8.4 aggregate math-score gains over PPO on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, plus improved out-of-distribution generalization across several model sizes and additional tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Because the method reconstructs values from position-wise outputs, implementation quality and calibration of the cumulative value logits may strongly affect stability under sparse-reward training.
infographic.paper_title: TPPO: Tracking-Value PPO For Language Model Reasoning

title: Towards Learning-Guided Discovery of Extremal Geometric Constructions: A PatternBoost Study
authors: Deepak Ajwani, Paula Carroll, Rishikesh Gajjala, Ananta Manoranjan, Ryan O'Connor, Rajiv Raman
abstract: Extremal constructions play a central role in the design and analysis of algorithms. Integrality-gap instances expose the limitations of relaxations, while hard configurations reveal structural sources of computational difficulty. Such constructions, however, are still typically discovered through a slow, manual process. This paper investigates how machine learning can accelerate their discovery to support algorithm design and analysis. We build on PatternBoost, a framework alternating local search with generation from a trained transformer, using its Axplorer implementation to investigate three problems: integrality gaps for maximum independent set of rectangles, integrality gaps for stabbing unit squares with axis-parallel lines, and hard instances for recursive guillotine cutting. By exploring candidate representations, local search operations, and surrogate models used to rank candidates before exact verification, we carefully adapt the framework to these combinatorial geometry problems.While naive representations and search strategies fail to find non-trivial instances, our tailored adaptation discovers numerous non-trivial constructions. For stabbing unit squares, the method reaches a gap of $20/13\approx 1.54$, improving on the literature's best known lower bound of $3/2$. Purely automated search converges rapidly and then plateaus, prompting the question of what is required to push the bound higher still. We find that initial instance diversity plays an important role: with modest expert input via a structured staircase construction, the system reaches an improved integrality gap of $14/9\approx 1.555$. These results demonstrate that machine learning and domain expertise can be combined to discover new extremal constructions that advance algorithmic lower bounds.

infographic.key_insight: PatternBoost, when adapted with geometry-aware representations and search moves, can automate the discovery of stronger extremal constructions than prior hand-designed efforts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study shows that learning-guided search can accelerate lower-bound discovery for combinatorial geometry problems, informing algorithm design and hardness analysis.
method: Alternate local search with transformer-generated candidate constructions.
Use tailored instance encodings plus surrogate ranking before exact verification.
Inject modest expert-crafted diversity when automated search plateaus.
infographic.evidence_signal: On stabbing unit squares with axis-parallel lines, the method improved the best known lower bound from 3/2 to 20/13, and with structured staircase initialization to 14/9.
infographic.watch_item: Performance appears sensitive to representation quality and initial diversity, so naive encodings or search operators may fail or plateau early.
infographic.paper_title: Towards Learning-Guided Discovery of Extremal Geometric Constructions: A PatternBoost Study

title: From Global to Tail Convergence: Dynamics of $α$-Stable Score-Based Generative Models
authors: Ianis Hammani, Claire Boyer
abstract: Score-based generative models driven by $α$-stable L{é}vy processes have been proposed as an alternative to Brownian diffusion models, with empirical evidence suggesting improved sampling and better modeling of heavy-tailed data. Yet theoretical guarantees for these models remain limited. We develop a non-asymptotic convergence analysis for scale-preserving $α$-stable generative dynamics, covering both compactly supported and power-law targets. In p-Wasserstein distance, we quantify the effects of early stopping, initialization, score approximation, and time discretization, and show exponential decay of the initialization error. A comparison with Brownian dynamics reveals that global Wasserstein convergence alone does not fundamentally distinguish the two models: both initialization errors decay exponentially with the forward horizon on the common class of heavy-tailed targets. A sharp separation emerges instead in the tails. At any positive generation time, stable dynamics produces power-law tails with index $α$, whereas Brownian dynamics remains light-tailed. For a target with tail index $ν$, asymptotically correct extreme-quantile scaling is possible precisely when $α$=$ν$. These results identify tail-index matching as a principled mechanism behind the ability of stable generative models to capture extreme events.

infographic.key_insight: α-stable score-based generative models match heavy-tailed targets by preserving power-law tails, and tail-index matching (α = ν) is the key condition for correct extreme-event scaling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For applications with rare but consequential extremes—such as risk modeling, anomaly generation, or climate/finance simulation—stable dynamics can better preserve tail behavior than Brownian diffusion models.
method: Non-asymptotic p-Wasserstein convergence analysis for scale-preserving α-stable generative dynamics
Quantification of initialization, early stopping, score approximation, and time-discretization errors
Comparison against Brownian dynamics to separate global convergence from tail behavior
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence bounds, exponential decay of initialization error, and tail asymptotics showing power-law tails for stable dynamics versus light tails for Brownian dynamics.
infographic.watch_item: Tail benefits depend on correct α–ν matching; mis-specifying the stability index or using approximate scores/discretization may degrade extreme-quantile fidelity.
infographic.paper_title: From Global to Tail Convergence: Dynamics of $α$-Stable Score-Based Generative Models

title: Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs
authors: Mattie Ji, Indradyumna Roy, Vikas Garg
abstract: Persistent homology summarizes the topological evolution of a graph as persistence diagrams (PDs). Generating graphs whose topology matches a target descriptor is increasingly important, yet existing topology-aware generative models rely on soft regularization, producing graphs whose PDs may only be approximately similar. We initiate a principled investigation of the generation problem: produce graphs that realize a target PD exactly. We propose two approaches guided by the implicit local and global constraints a target PD imposes. The local approach builds degree-based PD-equivalent graphs iteratively, and we prove that every output realizes the target PD and that every degree-based PD-equivalent graph is reachable. However, as shown thereafter, local generation necessarily trades off between sample diversity and reaching infeasible states. We therefore recast generation as a global constraint satisfaction problem with a complete encoding solvable by modern constraint programming solvers. This is applicable to any vertex-based permutation equivariant filtration scheme and is minimal under the degree filtration. Experiments on four standard graph generation benchmarks confirm that both methods realize the target PD exactly. Together, our methods provide a principled treatment of strict topology-compliant graph generation. Code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/ExactCompliance.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows how to generate graphs whose persistent homology matches a target persistence diagram exactly, rather than only approximately.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables topology-constrained graph synthesis for design and simulation pipelines where exact structural guarantees matter.
method: Local iterative generation of degree-based PD-equivalent graphs with provable exactness and reachability.
Global formulation as a complete constraint satisfaction problem solved by modern CP solvers.
Applies to any vertex-based permutation-equivariant filtration and is minimal under degree filtration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four standard graph generation benchmarks, both proposed methods produced graphs whose target persistence diagrams were matched exactly.
infographic.watch_item: The local method can trade off diversity and may encounter infeasible states, so solver-based global encoding may be preferable but could be more computationally demanding.
infographic.paper_title: Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs

title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification
authors: Rodney Lafuente-Mercado, Salman Rahman, Jingyan Shen, James Shiffer, Saadia Gabriel, Pavel Izmailov
abstract: AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. Given the labels need no human annotation, LeanPRM can grow with the supply of formal statements, offering a path to step-level feedback on AI-generated proofs that are hard for humans to check.

infographic.key_insight: LeanPRM turns Lean-formalized proofs into step-level supervision for natural-language proof verification without human annotations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a scalable recipe for training proof verifiers that can improve step checking and best-of-N proof selection across model sizes.
method: Generate a natural-language proof and a paired Lean formal proof without Lean feedback.
Use Lean to label each proof step as correct or incorrect.
Filter out syntax-only Lean failures with a second model so negatives reflect mathematical mistakes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The dataset includes 10,634 proofs and 152K labeled steps; a Qwen3-4B verifier improved exact step-label accuracy on LeanPRM-Bench from 48.2% to 74.7% and beat PRM800K training at 60.3%.
infographic.watch_item: The pipeline depends on the availability and quality of formal Lean statements and on a secondary model to separate syntactic failures from genuine math errors.
infographic.paper_title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification

title: Combining Post-Quantum Cryptography and Quantum Key Distribution: Taxonomy, Constructions, Proofs, Standards, Deployments and Open Problems
authors: Mona Alotaibi, Noora Fetais, Saif Al-Kuwari
abstract: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) address the quantum threat from opposite directions: PQC replaces vulnerable public-key algorithms with schemes believed to resist quantum cryptanalysis, while QKD derives keys whose secrecy rests on physical assumptions rather than computational ones. Because each approach has a distinct failure mode, a growing body of work combines them so that a session key remains secure if either component holds. We first establish the deployed baseline, hybrid classical-plus-PQC key exchange, against which QKD-augmented designs must be judged. We then propose a taxonomy of hybrid PQC-QKD designs along eight dimensions (integration layer, combiner construction, authentication scope and source, QKD topology, trusted entities, key-delivery interface, classical component, and evidence type), and use it to compare published protocols, including Muckle and its successors, MACsec and TLS integrations, and IKEv2 mechanisms standardised in RFCs 8784, 9370, and 9867. We examine key-combiner constructions in light of the KEM-combiner literature and of NIST, ETSI, and ITU-T guidance, and map the security arguments for hybrid PQC-QKD protocols onto a common grid of security model, assumptions, permitted compromise, established guarantee, and limitations. We synthesise deployment evidence from metropolitan and national QKD networks, distinguishing the few testbeds that have run PQC in the key path from pure-QKD deployments, and summarise the standards and policy landscape, including the positions of national security agencies that recommend against relying on QKD alone. We close with open problems: authentication of the QKD classical channel, shared-infrastructure threat models, device certification versus formal proofs, formal verification of hybrid handshakes, and the lack of peer-reviewed deployment economics.

infographic.key_insight: Hybrid PQC-QKD designs aim to keep session keys secure if either the computational layer or the physical quantum layer remains secure, but their real value depends on how the two components are combined and authenticated.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The paper gives engineers a practical taxonomy and comparison framework for selecting, standardizing, and deploying quantum-safe key exchange across TLS, MACsec, and IKEv2-style systems.
method: Define an 8-dimension taxonomy for PQC-QKD hybrids
Compare published protocols, standards, and combiner designs against a common security grid
Survey deployment evidence from QKD testbeds and networks
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract synthesizes protocol literature, standards guidance, and deployment reports, but does not present a new experimental benchmark or numerical evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: A major implementation concern is authenticating the QKD classical channel and proving security under shared-infrastructure and real-world deployment assumptions.
infographic.paper_title: Combining Post-Quantum Cryptography and Quantum Key Distribution: Taxonomy, Constructions, Proofs, Standards, Deployments and Open Problems

title: A Rate Transfer Method: Convergence Rates in Stochastic Gradient Descent via Stochastic Calculus
authors: Neil Walton
abstract: We develop a rate-transfer method that converts finite-time Lyapunov estimates for an associated stochastic differential equation (SDE) into finite-time convergence bounds for stochastic gradient algorithms. Under generic moment and smoothness conditions, the convergence analysis of the stochastic gradient method reduces to a calculus argument verifying a Lyapunov generator inequality for the SDE. The method recovers established rates for classical stochastic gradient methods and provides a way to establish convergence rates for new optimization algorithms through calculus arguments applied to their associated SDEs.

infographic.key_insight: The paper turns finite-time Lyapunov bounds for an associated SDE into convergence-rate guarantees for stochastic gradient algorithms via a rate-transfer method.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives practitioners a calculus-based route to prove or estimate optimization rates for new SGD-style methods without doing a full discrete-time analysis from scratch.
method: Construct an SDE that approximates or corresponds to the stochastic gradient algorithm.
Prove a finite-time Lyapunov generator inequality for the SDE using smoothness and moment assumptions.
Transfer the SDE bound into a finite-time convergence rate for the discrete algorithm.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the method recovers established rates for classical stochastic gradient methods and extends to new algorithms through calculus arguments.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on generic moment and smoothness conditions plus a valid SDE connection, so it may be less straightforward for highly non-smooth or strongly non-asymptotic implementations.
infographic.paper_title: A Rate Transfer Method: Convergence Rates in Stochastic Gradient Descent via Stochastic Calculus

title: Quantum Cryptography and Autoformalization in Lean
authors: Maor Ben Shahar, Jonathan Morag, Dirk Englund, Kfir Sulimany
abstract: Quantum key distribution provides secure communication by relying on physics principles and mathematical reasoning. Security proofs across the field can contain gaps, often between individually valid theorems integrated under mismatched assumptions. We produce an end-to-end security theorem formalized in the Lean proof assistant, eliminating hidden hypotheses by building only on Lean's standard axioms. Our proof covers composable security of the entanglement-based qubit BB84 protocol against coherent attacks by the postselection technique, accounting for finite block size, and is written in a language that enforces local operations and classical communication to help ensure a faithful representation of the protocol. The proof itself was enabled by LLM-based autoformalization, and with the proof complete, we used the same pipeline as a discovery machine, reducing the finite-size penalty on the key rate. Our work sets a reproducible standard for security arguments in quantum cryptography and shows how formal proof engines can accelerate discovery across quantum information science.

infographic.key_insight: They formalize an end-to-end security proof for entanglement-based BB84 in Lean, removing hidden assumptions and making the cryptographic argument machine-checkable.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a reproducible standard for quantum cryptography proofs and shows how formal methods can both verify security and help optimize finite-size key rates.
method: Formalized composable security of entanglement-based qubit BB84 against coherent attacks in Lean
Used the postselection technique to handle general attacks and finite block-size effects
Leveraged LLM-based autoformalization to build the proof and then reuse the pipeline for discovery
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a complete Lean formalization of the security theorem, with the same autoformalization pipeline also used to reduce the finite-size penalty on the key rate.
infographic.watch_item: Formal verification strengthens confidence, but the result still depends on the modeling choices, protocol encoding, and the finite-size assumptions used in the Lean specification.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Cryptography and Autoformalization in Lean

title: VASPO: Self-Distillation with Privileged Value Estimation
authors: Fei Wu, Zhenrong Zhang, Jianshu Zhang, Jun Du
abstract: On-policy self-distillation provides dense supervision for reasoning models via a privileged self-teacher. However, this supervision reflects local token preferences rather than the expected return of an unguided student continuation. Recent methods combine this signal with GRPO. They use GRPO for update directions and the teacher for signal scaling. However, we demonstrate a more effective integration within PPO. Specifically, we identify complementary positional dynamics: privileged information enhances a critic's value-prediction accuracy toward the response's end, whereas self-teacher guidance is strong initially, drops mid-generation, and rebounds finally. These insights motivate Value-Augmented Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (VASPO), wherein a self-teacher and critic evaluate identical privileged information at student-generated prefixes. The critic computes token-level PPO advantages from predicted continuation returns, while the self-teacher modulates selected positive advantages via bounded probability ratios. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VASPO improves mean accuracy over PPO by 2.59 and 1.81 percentage points on Qwen3-4B and OLMo3-7B variants, respectively, and achieves the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods on Knights and Knaves. Our code is available at https://github.com/cii030/VASPO.

infographic.key_insight: VASPO combines a critic and a self-teacher at the same student-generated prefixes to better align self-distillation with expected return, improving reasoning policy optimization over PPO.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For math-reasoning model training, VASPO offers a practical way to mix value-based credit assignment with privileged self-teaching, yielding stronger and more stable updates than using self-distillation alone.
method: Critic estimates token-level PPO advantages from predicted continuation returns.
Self-teacher uses privileged information to scale selected positive advantages with bounded probability ratios.
Designed around positional dynamics: critic improves toward the end of generations, while self-teacher is strongest early and late.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VASPO improved mean accuracy over PPO by 2.59 points on Qwen3-4B and 1.81 points on OLMo3-7B, and achieved the best mean accuracy on Knights and Knaves.
infographic.watch_item: Because VASPO relies on privileged information and bounded ratio-based scaling, its gains may depend on careful synchronization of teacher and critic signals to avoid unstable updates.
infographic.paper_title: VASPO: Self-Distillation with Privileged Value Estimation

title: Large-Step Last-Iterate Convergence of Random-Reshuffling Stochastic Gradient Descent
authors: Zijun Chen, Zihan Zhang
abstract: Random reshuffling stochastic gradient descent (RR-SGD) is widely used for finite-sum optimization in machine learning. For convex $L$-smooth components, recent work establishes convergence guarantees for an averaged iterate with component stepsizes as large as order $1/L$. However, the final iterate is a natural output in practice, and existing last-iterate guarantees in this setting require stepsizes that scale inversely with the number of components $n$. We establish an expected objective-gap bound for the last iterate of standard RR-SGD on unconstrained problems with a constant component stepsize satisfying $0<η\lesssim 1/(L(1 + \log(nK)))$, where $K$ is the number of epochs. By retaining the sampling bias at random comparison points, we remove the explicit $1/n$ factor from the stepsize restriction. Combined with existing small-step bounds, our result matches the corresponding averaged-iterate convergence rate up to logarithmic factors.

infographic.key_insight: Random-reshuffling SGD can guarantee convergence of the final iterate with a much larger constant stepsize than prior last-iterate results, removing the usual explicit 1/n restriction up to logarithmic factors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes RR-SGD more practical for large finite-sum machine learning problems because the naturally returned last model iterate can be used without requiring overly tiny per-component stepsizes.
method: Analyze unconstrained finite-sum optimization with convex, L-smooth component losses.
Retain the sampling bias at random comparison points in the proof to avoid the explicit 1/n stepsize dependence.
Combine the new last-iterate bound with existing small-step results to match averaged-iterate rates up to log factors.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an expected objective-gap bound for the RR-SGD last iterate with constant component stepsize η ≲ 1/(L(1 + log(nK))), where K is the number of epochs.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantee is logarithmically weakened and applies to unconstrained convex L-smooth finite-sum problems, so its direct use in nonconvex or constrained settings is not implied.
infographic.paper_title: Large-Step Last-Iterate Convergence of Random-Reshuffling Stochastic Gradient Descent

title: Output Discipline Sets the Floor: A Falsification-Guided, Model-Agnostic Agent Protocol for Auditable Hypothesis-Driven Decision Making
authors: Jing Liu, Yongxing Qi, Ping Yao, Ting Wu
abstract: What binds large language models on auditable, hypothesis-driven decision tasks, where every candidate can be checked against the evidence? On the public TCMEval-SDT benchmark for Traditional Chinese Medicine syndrome differentiation (200 cases), the binding constraint is output discipline and reasoning structure, not model capability alone: two years of model scaling move zero-shot scores by only -0.03 to +0.08, while output-discipline failures (non-terminating reasoning, format non-compliance, large run-to-run spread) persist even in frontier models. We test this with a model-agnostic agent framework formalizing decision making as a five-stage closed loop, enforced by a candidate x evidence matrix falsification protocol: every candidate is judged against every evidence item, at least half of the candidates must be falsified before a conclusion is licensed, and survivors are emitted in a machine-verifiable single-line format. Across five base models, the effect is sign-conditional on zero-shot output discipline: it rescues models whose discipline fails (DeepSeek-V4-Flash: +0.267/+0.271, entirely termination rescue), reduces a high-variance model's run-to-run standard deviation from 0.218 to 0.007 (Kimi K3), and significantly costs already-disciplined models (-0.087 to -0.120 on budget-matched Qwen3-4B/32B). Ablations attribute the cost to the candidate-bounded format layer and show the effect is independent of injected knowledge content (protocol-knowledge decoupling). The protocol also transfers to misinformation-robust mathematical reasoning, detecting injected false premises at 89.8% recall with a 6.8% false-positive rate (MCC 0.54; a flag-everything baseline scores 0) and restoring accuracy to the no-misinformation ceiling. Where zero-shot output discipline is weak, the reasoning protocol sets the floor; base-model capability always sets the ceiling.

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that in auditable, hypothesis-driven decision tasks, output discipline and structured reasoning matter more than raw model scale, and a falsification-guided protocol can rescue weak models while exposing the limits of already-disciplined ones.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For dependable agent systems, the key design target is not only better models but enforceable output formats, explicit candidate-vs-evidence checking, and termination guarantees that make decisions machine-verifiable.
method: Five-stage closed-loop agent protocol for decision making
Candidate × evidence matrix with falsification of every candidate against every evidence item
License a conclusion only after at least half the candidates are falsified and survivors are emitted in a single-line verifiable format
infographic.evidence_signal: On TCMEval-SDT (200 cases), the protocol improved weak models by about +0.27, reduced one model’s run-to-run standard deviation from 0.218 to 0.007, and transferred to misinformation-robust math reasoning with 89.8% recall and 6.8% false-positive rate.
infographic.watch_item: The protocol can reduce accuracy on already disciplined models, so implementation should be budget-aware and benchmarked against format overhead and task-specific failure modes.
infographic.paper_title: Output Discipline Sets the Floor: A Falsification-Guided, Model-Agnostic Agent Protocol for Auditable Hypothesis-Driven Decision Making

title: Scaling Multilingual Safety and Reasoning Evaluation through Reasoning-Guided Translation
authors: Zahraa Al Sahili, Ioannis Patras, Matthew Purver
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across languages, yet their safety and reasoning capabilities remain predominantly evaluated in English. Translating existing benchmarks offers a scalable approach to multilingual evaluation, but preserving task-specific meaning across languages presents significant challenges, particularly for harmful requests, mathematical reasoning, and conversational interactions. We introduce a reasoning-guided translation framework for constructing multilingual evaluations designed to preserve the structure and intended meaning of diverse benchmark tasks. Our approach separates translation strategy selection from large-scale generation, combining reasoning-guided configuration selection with task-aware validation, targeted repair, and independent quality screening. Using this framework, we develop a source-aligned evaluation collection spanning seven safety, conversational, and mathematical reasoning resources across 11 languages. The resulting collection achieves 99.94\% coverage of intended item--language pairs in the two subsets requiring repair. Evaluations of open-source LLMs reveal distinct language-dependent vulnerabilities, including inconsistent refusal behaviour and substantial reasoning degradation in lower-resource languages. These findings highlight the importance of task-sensitive benchmark construction and systematic quality assessment for understanding multilingual model behaviour beyond English.

infographic.key_insight: Reasoning-guided translation can preserve benchmark meaning across languages, enabling more reliable multilingual safety and mathematical reasoning evaluation than direct translation alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This framework provides a scalable way to build high-quality multilingual test sets for evaluating LLM behavior in safety-critical and reasoning-heavy applications beyond English.
method: Select translation strategies with reasoning guidance before generation
Apply task-aware validation, targeted repair, and independent quality screening
Assemble source-aligned benchmarks across safety, conversation, and math resources in 11 languages
infographic.evidence_signal: The resulting collection covers 99.94% of intended item–language pairs in the two subsets that required repair, and evaluations show language-dependent refusal inconsistencies and reasoning drops in lower-resource languages.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark quality still depends on preserving task intent during translation, so low-resource languages and culturally sensitive harmful prompts may remain harder to validate consistently.
infographic.paper_title: Scaling Multilingual Safety and Reasoning Evaluation through Reasoning-Guided Translation

title: Optimization for One, Feasibility for Most: Decoupling Optimization from Feasibility in Chance-Constrained Programs
authors: Justin Dumouchelle, Shunyu Yao, Beste Basciftci, Thiago Serra
abstract: Chance-constrained stochastic programs (CCSPs) require solutions that satisfy uncertain constraints with high probability. Standard approaches either embed scenarios directly into optimization by considering sample average approximation (SAA)-based reformulations, growing prohibitively expensive and often failing to find feasible solutions; or employ conservative reformulations that guarantee feasibility but sacrifice objective quality by design. We propose ACCESS (Adaptive Chance-Constrained Exploration via Structured Sampling), a structured sampling framework that decouples optimization from feasibility evaluation. First, high-quality candidate solutions are generated by solving many inexpensive single-scenario subproblems, avoiding sampling directly in the constrained high-dimensional solution space. Second, feasibility is assessed separately via large-scale batched simulation over a massive number of scenarios, which is naturally amenable to GPU parallelism. That reduces the search from a high-dimensional solution space to a two-dimensional parameter space controlling conservatism and scenario diversity; while concentrating on candidates near the feasibility boundary, where high-quality feasible solutions lie. We also introduce a variant, ACCESS($δ$), which provides certified feasibility guarantees with probability $1-δ$. Experiments across three benchmark classes and five scenario distributions show that ACCESS matches or exceeds the best objective found by any method in nearly every setting, while ACCESS($δ$) is empirically feasible on every instance. The conservative reformulations remain several percent worse in objective, and SAA is frequently infeasible while taking an order of magnitude longer on the harder benchmarks.

infographic.key_insight: ACCESS decouples finding strong candidate solutions from checking feasibility, using many cheap single-scenario solves plus large-scale batched simulation instead of expensive all-at-once scenario optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This can make chance-constrained optimization practical for large stochastic design and operations problems by improving solution quality while reducing compute and leveraging GPU-parallel feasibility testing.
method: Generate candidate solutions from many inexpensive single-scenario subproblems rather than embedding all scenarios in one high-dimensional solve.
Evaluate feasibility separately with massive batched Monte Carlo simulation, which is highly parallel on GPUs.
Focus search on a 2D tradeoff space of conservatism and scenario diversity, with ACCESS(δ) adding probabilistic feasibility certification.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three benchmark classes and five scenario distributions, ACCESS matched or exceeded the best objective in nearly every setting, while ACCESS(δ) was empirically feasible on every instance and SAA was often infeasible and much slower on harder cases.
infographic.watch_item: The approach relies on simulation-based feasibility assessment and tuning of conservatism/diversity, so certification and performance may depend on sampling budget, distribution shift, and problem structure.
infographic.paper_title: Optimization for One, Feasibility for Most: Decoupling Optimization from Feasibility in Chance-Constrained Programs
